newsitem.title: FRANCE: Change in Ffr-mark parity seen unlikely-economists.
newsitem.headline: Change in Ffr-mark parity seen unlikely-economists.

text.p: Comments on Thursday by a Bank of France council member raising questions about exchange rate policy do not herald a franc devaluation, economists said.
"I don't think it (the debate) will end with devaluation but with a fall in German interest rates that will not be preceded by a fall in French rates," said BFCE economist Francois Chevalier.

The franc fell sharply after council member Jean-Pierre Gerrard said that while the current franc-mark rate posed no problems, German lack of understading on monetary and exchange rate policy could make a change in the parity necessary.
"I cannot see France embarking on a different monetary policy," said economist Marie Owens-Thomsen of BIP.
At 1154 GMT, the franc was trading at 3.3933 per mark, above its lows of 3.3972 touched just after Gerard's comments but three-quarters of a centime below its intraday high of 3.3857 per mark.
Economists said the market's nervousness over latest events had been exacerbated by jitters about two appointments to be made to the Bank's nine-person monetary policy council by year end.
Of the nine council members, six are seen as monetary policy hawks, the newspaper Liberation reported on Wednesday. Of those, the mandates of two expire at year-end but can be renewed.

The three others, including Gerard and Paul Marchelli, who spoke out earlier in the week urging that Europe avoid launching a single currency that was too strong against the dollar, are viewed as doves, Liberation said.
The speakers of the upper and lower houses of parliament and the head of the Economic and Social Council name six people for the two vacancies out of which the government will make its choice.

The three, National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin who spearheaded the campaign against the Maastricht treaty, Senate speaker Rene Monory and Jean Matteoli, president of the consultative Economic and Social Council, have made no comment on their nominees.

Economists said it was unlikely that the centre-right government would shift the balance radically to tip it against Bank governor Jean-Claude Trichet, who has championed France's decade-old franc fort policy. "I don't think they will shift the balance, but it (the changes) could make Trichet's majority less comfortable," one economist said.

Those who watch the Bank of France closely said that Marchelli and Gerard were still in the minority in calling for faster rate cuts. On Thursday the Bank announced it was holding rates unchanged after its regular council meeting.

"I am not so convinced it (the changes) will weaken it (the Bank of France) so substantially as to change fundamentally the policy mix of the Bank of France council going forward into 1997," said Credit Lyonnais bond analyst Iain Lindsay.

The comments by Gerard and Marchelli, bringing into the open divisions on the central bank council, have come on top of calls by former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing urging a weaker currency to revive the flagging economy and bring down unemployment, now at a record 12.6 percent.
